description: End-to-end interview blueprints: Design Twitter/X Newsfeed (Fan-out on write vs read), WhatsApp / Telegram Chat Architecture, and Instagram Photo Sharing.

topics.title: Case Study: Design Twitter / X Newsfeed (Fan-Out on Write vs Read)
topics.definition: Design a distributed real-time newsfeed system capable of handling 500 million Daily Active Users (DAU), 500 million tweets/day, and delivering customized chronological / ranked feeds with sub-200ms latency.
topics.why_we_need_it: The definitive classic system design interview problem testing distributed caching, fan-out architectures, and handling extreme celebrity skew (Justin Bieber / Elon Musk problem).
topics.real_world_analogy: A physical newspaper delivery vs a library corkboard: Fan-out on write is delivering a copy of your flyer into every follower's home mailbox the moment you write it. Fan-out on read is tacking the flyer on a central corkboard and making followers walk to the library to scan and assemble their own feed.
topics.how_it_works:
1. Fan-out on Write (Push Model): When User A posts a tweet, background workers look up User A's followers and inject the tweet ID into every follower's in-memory Redis Home Timeline list (`LPUSH timeline:user_id tweet_id`). Reading feed is a lightning-fast `O(1)` Redis `LRANGE` operation.
2. The Celebrity Problem: If an account with 100 million followers tweets, fan-out on write requires 100 million Redis writes, locking servers and taking minutes.
3. Hybrid Fan-out Architecture (Production Solution): Normal users use Fan-out on Write. Celebrity users (>50,000 followers) bypass fan-out on write. When a user requests their feed, the system fetches their precomputed Redis feed AND dynamically fetches tweets from the few celebrities they follow (Fan-out on Read), merging the two lists in memory.
conceptual_breakdown: Twitter Scale Math: 500M DAU, 500M tweets/day = 6,000 tweets/sec avg (20,000 peak). Read QPS = 300,000 QPS (50:1 read/write ratio).
Storage: Tweet metadata in PostgreSQL/DynamoDB; User timelines in Redis clusters (storing 800 most recent tweet IDs per active user in RAM).
Media: Photos and videos uploaded directly to S3 via Presigned URLs, served via Global CDN.

topics.failure_scenarios: Inactive User Redis RAM Bloat: Precomputing timelines for 500 million registered users who haven't logged in for 3 years wastes terabytes of expensive RAM. Mitigation: Only precompute timelines for users who were active within the last 14 days (Lazy loading on login for inactive users).

common_mistakes.mistake: Using pure Fan-out on Read (`SELECT * FROM tweets WHERE user_id IN (following_ids) ORDER BY created_at DESC`) for all 500 million users.
common_mistakes.correction: This generates catastrophic multi-million row JOIN queries under 300,000 QPS. Use the Hybrid Fan-Out model.

interview_questions.question: How does Twitter handle the 'Celebrity Fan-out Problem' in production?
interview_questions.answer: Twitter uses a Hybrid approach: tweets from normal users are pushed into their followers' Redis timelines immediately on write (Fan-out on Write). Tweets from celebrity accounts with millions of followers bypass fan-out on write; instead, when a user opens their feed, the system dynamically pulls and merges the latest tweets from any celebrities that user follows (Fan-out on Read).

topics.title: Case Study: Design WhatsApp / Messenger (1-on-1 & Group Chat Architecture)
topics.definition: Design a globally distributed instant messaging platform supporting 2 billion users, end-to-end encryption (Signal Protocol), 100 billion messages/day, online presence status, and group messaging.
topics.why_we_need_it: Tests persistent bi-directional WebSocket connection management, ephemeral message delivery pipelines, distributed presence tracking, and offline message storage.
topics.real_world_analogy: A dedicated pneumatic tube system between every pair of office desks: when you drop a capsule in, it shoots instantly to your colleague's desk if they are sitting there. If their desk is empty, the capsule drops into their locked drawer until they return.
topics.how_it_works:
1. Connection Gateway: Millions of mobile clients maintain persistent TCP/WebSocket connections to a fleet of distributed Chat Gateway servers (e.g. built with Erlang/Elixir BEAM or Netty).
2. User Session Registry: A distributed Redis cluster maps `user_id -> Gateway_Server_ID` (e.g., `Alice -> Gateway-14`, `Bob -> Gateway-89`).
3. Message Delivery Flow (1-on-1): Alice sends message to Gateway-14. Gateway looks up Bob in Session Registry -> forwards message to Gateway-89 -> Gateway-89 pushes message down Bob's active WebSocket connection.
4. Offline Queue: If Bob is offline, message is stored in an ephemeral Cassandra/DynamoDB offline queue. When Bob reconnects, he pulls all pending offline messages, and the server deletes them upon ACK.
5. Group Chat: Group service expands group membership list and creates individual fan-out delivery jobs for each member.
conceptual_breakdown: End-to-End Encryption (E2EE): WhatsApp servers CANNOT read message contents; servers only route encrypted ciphertext blobs between public keys.
Message Statuses: Single Tick (Sent to server), Double Grey Tick (Delivered to recipient phone), Blue Double Tick (Read by user).
Presence Engine: Heartbeat pings every 30s update Redis TTL key `presence:{user_id}`.
topics.failure_scenarios: Massive Group Chat Message Multiplication: A group with 1,000 members where 50 users are texting simultaneously generates $50 \times 1,000 = 50,000$ messages per second. Mitigation: Client-side group message pulling and batching via Kafka topics.
